items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the complex numbers [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2,] given by

Content:
[MATH: z_1=a+\textrm i b , \qquad
z_2=c+\textrm i d.]

Content:
Suppose we wish to compute the distance between these two numbers in the complex plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4848f265c4e74c5e47b183451f71e7af]

Content:
By the distance formula, the distance [MATH: D] between these two complex numbers is given by

Content:
[MATH: D = \sqrt{(a-c)^2+(b-d)^2}.]

Content:
However, notice that

Content:
[MATH: z_{1} − z_{2}|= (a + b\textrm{i}) − (c + d\textrm{i}); = (a − c) + (b − d)\textrm{i},]

Content:
and therefore,

Content:
[MATH: |z_1 - z_2 | = \sqrt{(a-c)^2+(b-d)^2} .]

Content:
To summarize, the distance between two numbers in the complex plane equals the modulus of the difference between the numbers:

Content:
[MATH: D = |z_1-z_2| = \sqrt{(a-c)^2 + (b-d)^2}]

[MATH: z_{1} = 1 + \textrm{i}, z_{2} = 2 + 3\textrm{i}]

Content:

Content:

Content:
Given two complex numbers

Content:
[MATH: z_1 = a+\textrm i b, \qquad z_2 = c+\textrm i d,]

Content:
we can calculate the number corresponding to the midpoint of the line segment joining [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] by taking the average of the two numbers:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{z_1 + z_2}{2} = \left( \dfrac{a+c}{2} \right) + \textrm i\left( \dfrac{b+d}{2} \right)]

Content:
Notice that this formula is analogous to the midpoint formula in the cartesian plane. In the case of complex numbers [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2,] we take the average of the real and imaginary parts of the two numbers.

Content:
For example, let's calculate the midpoint of the segment with endpoints [MATH: z_1 = 2+\textrm i] and [MATH: z_2 = 4+5\textrm i.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f3fe005160a3a65368a214dd073a8f9e]

Content:
The midpoint is given by

Content:
[MATH: (z_{1} + z_{2})/(2)|= ((2 + \textrm{i}) + (4 + 5\textrm{i}))/(2); = (6 + 6\textrm{i})/(2); = 3 + 3\textrm{i}.]

Content:

items.readable_text:
Content:
A median of a triangle is a line segment that connects a vertex of the triangle with the midpoint of the opposite side. Every triangle has precisely three medians, one for each vertex.

Content:
It can be shown that the medians intersect at a single point inside the triangle. This point of intersection is called the centroid (or center) of the triangle.

Content:
Given three complex numbers [MATH: z_1, z_2,] and [MATH: z_3] in the complex plane, the number corresponding to the centroid of the triangle with vertices [MATH: z_1, z_2, z_3] is the average of these numbers:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{z_1+z_2+z_3}{3}]

Content:
For example, let's calculate the number corresponding to the centroid of the triangle with vertices

Content:
[MATH: z_{1} = 1 + \textrm{i}, z_{2} = 5 + \textrm{i}, z_{3} = 4\textrm{i}.]

Content:
Our triangle is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/abb1e3c822897a580066c223dd61bc4f]

Content:
The location of the centroid corresponds to the complex number

Content:
[MATH: (z_{1} + z_{2} + z_{3})/(3)|= ((1 + \textrm{i}) + (5 + \textrm{i}) + (4\textrm{i}))/(3); = (6 + 6\textrm{i})/(3); = 2 + 2\textrm{i}.]

Content:
Our triangle and its centroid are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d761cc54ff1d0942345bea0ea569e1bb]

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Midpoint of a Line Segment in the Complex Plane

Content:
Given two complex numbers

Content:

Content:
we can calculate the number corresponding to the midpoint of the line segment joining [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2] by taking the average of the two numbers:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{z_1 + z_2}{2} = \left( \dfrac{a+c}{2} \right) + \textrm i\left( \dfrac{b+d}{2} \right)]

Content:
Notice that this formula is analogous to the midpoint formula in the cartesian plane. In the case of complex numbers [MATH: z_1] and [MATH: z_2,] we take the average of the real and imaginary parts of the two numbers.

[MATH: (z_{1} + z_{2})/(2)|= ((2 + \textrm{i}) + (4 + 5\textrm{i}))/(2); = (6 + 6\textrm{i})/(2); = 3 + 3\textrm{i}.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Centroid of a Triangle

Content:
A median of a triangle is a line segment that connects a vertex of the triangle with the midpoint of the opposite side. Every triangle has precisely three medians, one for each vertex.

Content:
It can be shown that the medians intersect at a single point inside the triangle. This point of intersection is called the centroid (or center) of the triangle.

Content:
Given three complex numbers [MATH: z_1, z_2,] and [MATH: z_3] in the complex plane, the number corresponding to the centroid of the triangle with vertices [MATH: z_1, z_2, z_3] is the average of these numbers:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{z_1+z_2+z_3}{3}]

Content:
For example, let's calculate the number corresponding to the centroid of the triangle with vertices

Content:
[MATH: z_{1} = 1 + \textrm{i}, z_{2} = 5 + \textrm{i}, z_{3} = 4\textrm{i}.]

The location of the centroid corresponds to the complex number

Content:
[MATH: (z_{1} + z_{2} + z_{3})/(3)|= ((1 + \textrm{i}) + (5 + \textrm{i}) + (4\textrm{i}))/(3); = (6 + 6\textrm{i})/(3); = 2 + 2\textrm{i}.]
